entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: 1 epoch + 64 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same network and sample count as the 1-epoch candidate (about 405k steps), but with 64 minibatches of 64 samples. This doubles the gradient steps per update at no extra compute, making up for each sample being used only once. It tests whether gradient steps rather than samples limit learning at 1 epoch. Refuted if it scores no better than r3c3's 0.785, or below the plain 1-epoch candidate by more than seed noise.
entries.last_analysis: Two changes clearly helped. First, a learned full-width circular (1,X) convolution on the target-side channels undoes the 4-column roll; alone it lifted dev success from 0 to 0.21. Second, more training samples helped far more than anything else. Removing the axial block brought r down from 1.52 to 1.05, and with 4 PPO epochs dev success rose to 0.50. Cutting to 2 epochs then gave 0.785, with both seeds close (0.81 and 0.76). The training curve was still rising at the end (0.73). Dev readouts show IoU 0.97 and exact builds on both diagnostic designs, so the remaining errors are small. Both data-heavy trials ran about 70 seconds, so time is not a constraint. An entropy bonus of 0.03 prevented collapse to pressing DONE straight away; 128 envs with entropy 0.01 collapsed. This last round keeps the r3c3 network and uses ppo_epochs 1, giving about 405k steps and about 99 updates. The three candidates differ in how they make up for using each sample once: plain, more minibatches, or a higher learning rate.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: best net, 64 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c2, but with 64 minibatches of 64 samples instead of 32 of 128. That doubles the gradient steps per update again while the sample count stays near 225k. Going from 16 to 32 minibatches raised dev success from 0.63 to 0.89, and training success was still rising, so gradient steps still seem to be the limit. Refuted if the 2-seed dev mean falls below about 0.85.
entries.last_analysis: Every observed target is shifted by X/2 columns. Rolling the input to undo that shift is what took dev success from 0 to about 0.6 (r1c1, r1c2). After that, the recipe mattered more than the architecture. Doubling the minibatches from 16 to 32 raised the score from 0.63 to 0.89 (r3c2, both seeds above 0.85), which is well beyond the seed spread. Raising entropy from 0.02 to 0.04 at 16 minibatches gave 0.74, a likely gain of about 0.1. Changes that made the network wider or the head more complex scored worse (r1c3, r2c1, r3c1). Using 1 PPO epoch or a longer horizon hurt badly (r2c2, r2c3). So the limit is gradient steps per sample plus early exploration, not network capacity. The remaining failures are wrong upper-layer bricks on tall stacks and early DONE, and training success was still rising at the end. This last round keeps the r3c2 network and tests: 64 minibatches alone, entropy 0.04 at 32 minibatches, and both together.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and their training success was also 0. That held for local footprint heads, per-layer heads, flat Linear heads (which can learn any mapping from actions to cells), cheap and expensive networks, and 1 to 4 epochs. Since the flat head failed too, a twist in the action indexing alone is unlikely to explain it. A permutation of observation channels is also unlikely, because the generic 1x1 stems would cope with it. The most likely common cause is that the policy collapses early. A random placement usually earns a negative reward because it fills cells outside the target. DONE, a single action that ends the episode, then looks better than the average placement, so PPO with lr 1e-3 and low entropy (0.005 in most trials) may lock into pressing DONE early. The greedy evaluation would then build nothing. With the last 3 trials, I am testing stability and exploration: lower lr, higher entropy and a longer horizon. I am also trying a network that sees the action mask.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are shown, so these choices rest on reasoning, not results. All 9 trials trained without errors, and the compute ratio r for every network stayed near 1, so there is room for small changes. Two ideas were tested separately but never together. One is the cell head with the stem skip (r3c1), which keeps exact per-column detail for each footprint cell. The other is 2 PPO epochs, which gives about 1.8x more fresh designs (r2c1, r3c2). Since there is no feedback and this is the last round, I am betting on combinations that each look reasonable, not on single-change tests. Combination 1: stem-skip cell head with 2 epochs. Combination 2: the same network with 1 epoch, which pushes sample count further (about 420k steps). Combination 3: add a dilated residual convolution, so every cell sees most of the 8x8 grid. That should help with placement order around overhangs and with DONE timing, at a modest cost.

entries.label: r2c1
entries.name: mirror + 2 PPO epochs
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. The budget then allows about 227k steps (about 110 updates) instead of about 158k. r1c2's training success was still rising when training stopped, so more fresh designs should help more than reusing each sample a third time. Refuted if dev success falls below 0.86, meaning the third epoch mattered more than the extra samples.
entries.last_analysis: Joining the trunk features with their left-right flip is what made the task learnable (0 to about 0.9). On the recipe side, 128 envs and 2 PPO epochs give the best result (r2c1, 0.919). Recipes that push for more, smaller updates (1 epoch; 64 envs) collapsed to pressing DONE straight away, scoring 0 on both seeds. Collapse to DONE is the main risk. A deeper trunk and global context in the head did not help. Gamma 0.99 gave the best single seed (0.953) but its two seeds were far apart (0.95 and 0.79). This last round keeps r2c1's sample budget and tries to make training less likely to collapse: orthogonal initialisation that starts the policy close to uniform, higher entropy, and gamma 0.99 with that initialisation. These are low-risk changes aimed at beating 0.919.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: r3c1 + lr 0.0015
entries.hypothesis: Combine the two improvements, 64 minibatches and a larger lr, at a moderate lr of 0.0015. Each sample then moves the policy further while the curve is still rising, so success should go above 0.933. A full lr of 0.002 on top of twice as many steps may be unstable, hence this middle value. Refuted if the mean is below 0.92 or one seed collapses.
entries.last_analysis: The big gain came from fixing the mirrored action layout. Cutting PPO epochs from 4 to 2, so the same budget buys more samples, added about 13 points. One epoch failed: the policy was under-fitted and one seed came out at 0.08. Within the 2-epoch recipe, both stronger optimisation changes helped by about 5 points over 0.877. Doubling the minibatches scored 0.933 with very consistent seeds; lr 0.002 scored 0.929. Learning curves were still rising at the end, so learning speed per sample is the bottleneck. The architecture changes either cost samples (two-stage head) or were unstable (stem skip: 0.92 and 0.32). Adding layers would cut samples, so this last round puts the trials into faster learning on the best network. Two candidates combine 64 minibatches with a larger lr (moderate and bold). The third keeps 64-sample minibatches but halves n_envs, which gives fresher rollouts and twice as many updates.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored 0 on every seed, and training success also stayed at 0. That held across every head type (footprint pooling, gather, per-layer, footprint-kernel, 3x3 conv, attention), across depths, and across recipes (1–2 epochs, 140k–400k steps, gamma 0.95–0.99). When nothing learns even on training designs, the cause is probably something every design shares, not capacity. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. Every head so far assumes that action index t*Y*X + y*X + x is the logit at feature cell (y, x). If the world transposes, flips or interleaves this order (cell-major instead of type-major), no spatially equivariant head can learn it. The 3x3 head only covers small shifts. This round tests heads that work under any convention: one sums logit maps over all orientations and both index orders, one adds a fully connected head that can learn any mapping, and one combines both.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: I can't see any scores, so I can't say which trial is best. The only evidence is that all 9 trials trained without errors, and that r3c2 shows a small network can run about 365k steps within the time limit. The remaining choices therefore rest on reasoning about the task. A brick placement is exact only if every cell under its footprint tops out at the same layer and the target is missing a cell at that layer in every one of them. The r3c3 head keeps each footprint cell separate, so it can learn this rule directly; pooling over the footprint loses which cell is which. Fresh random designs make more samples (1 epoch) a plausible gain for generalising to unseen designs, and wider context helps with build order. In this last round I combine these likely-good parts in different ways, which raises the chance that one 2-seed score beats the starting architecture. I don't change anything that is risky for the checks or the time limit.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

STEM = 64
COL = 48
WIDTH = 40
PROJ = 32
HID = 32


class PoolHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c, footprints, proj, hid):
        super().__init__()
        self.fps = [(int(a), int(b)) for a, b in footprints]
        self.proj = nn.Conv2d(c, proj, 1)
        self.mix = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv2d(3 * proj, hid, 1) for _ in self.fps])
        self.outs = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv2d(hid, 1, 1) for _ in self.fps])

    def forward(self, f):
        p = self.proj(f)
        res = []
        for (dy, dx), mix, out in zip(self.fps, self.mix, self.outs):
            if dy * dx == 1:
                mx, mn, av = p, p, p
            else:
                q = F.pad(p, (0, dx - 1, 0, dy - 1))
                mx = F.max_pool2d(q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
                mn = -F.max_pool2d(-q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
                av = F.avg_pool2d(q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
            h = F.relu(mix(torch.cat([mx, mn, av], dim=1)))
            res.append(out(h))
        return torch.cat(res, dim=1).flatten(1)


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(spec.in_channels, STEM, 1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(STEM, COL, 1), nn.ReLU())
        self.c1 = nn.Conv2d(COL, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.head = PoolHead(WIDTH, spec.footprints, PROJ, HID)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, 64), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(64, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(64, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        s = self.stem(obs)
        x = F.relu(self.c1(s))
        f = F.relu(x + self.c2(x))
        place = self.head(f)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)
